title: Cloud Audit Logging
summary: Cloud audit logging records the control-plane activity of a cloud account: which identity called which API, from which address, at what time, with which parameters, and with what result. Providers emit these events natively, and the records are the primary evidence for detection, investigation and compliance in cloud environments. Two properties shape how teams use them. Coverage varies, because control-plane events are usually recorded by default while data-plane events such as object reads or database queries often need explicit enablement and cost extra. Log storage is itself a security problem, because credentials with account access can frequently delete or disable the destination, so mature designs centralise logs into a separate account or an immutable store with tightly restricted write access. Audit logs support detections such as newly created administrative keys, policy changes, logging being switched off, and access from unexpected locations. The common mistake is switching logging on and never verifying that records actually arrive, that integrity validation is enabled, and that somebody watches for the obvious evasion attempts.

beginner.definition: Cloud audit logging means writing down every action taken in your cloud account. Each entry says who did it, what they did, when, and from which address. It is like a visitor book for the control panel of your cloud. If something goes wrong, this book tells you what happened.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who steals a cloud account leaves traces in these logs before they touch your data. Without logs you cannot tell what they copied or which keys they created. Auditors and regulators often ask for these records as proof that your controls work. Logs also answer simple questions, such as who deleted a database on Friday night. Losing them means losing the story of the incident.
howItWorks: Every request to the cloud control panel, whether from a person or a script, is recorded by the provider.
Each record lists the identity, the action, the time, the source address and whether the request succeeded.
The provider delivers these records to a storage location that you choose, usually within a few minutes.
You copy them into a separate account or a log platform, so nobody can delete them from the source account.
Detection rules and dashboards read the stream and raise alerts for patterns such as new administrator keys.
You keep the records for the period your policy or regulator requires, and protect them with restricted access.
beginner.example: Think of the sign in book at a secure library desk. Everyone who enters writes their name, the time, and which room they will use. The librarian keeps the book, not the visitor, so nobody can tear out a page later. If a rare manuscript goes missing, the librarian reads back through the entries for that evening. Cloud audit logging is that book for your cloud account. The provider writes each entry, and you keep a copy where the visitor cannot reach it.
takeaways: Store audit logs in a separate account or system, because an attacker with account access can delete them.
Check which events are recorded by default, since many data level actions need extra settings.
Treat a sudden gap in the log as an alert, because it may mean someone is covering their tracks.

objectives: Explain what cloud audit logging records and which questions it can answer.
Describe the difference between control plane actions and data plane actions in an audit log.
Outline how to centralise logs so they survive compromise of the source account.
Identify detection use cases that are built on audit log data.
Explain retention, integrity and access requirements for audit records.
